extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent examiners and design-patent practitioners (applicants/attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining whether multiple embodiments, combinations/subcombinations, or differing scopes in a design application are patentably distinct (requiring restriction under 35 U.S.C. 121) or patentably indistinct (may be retained in one application). Includes required examiner actions and applicant response rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple embodiments permitted only if single inventive concept / patentably indistinct
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple embodiments of a single inventive concept may be included in the same design application only if they are patentably indistinct. Embodiments that are patentably distinct from one another do not constitute a single inventive concept and thus may not be included in the same design application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite: In re Rubinfield, In re Platner. Examiner should determine whether embodiments are patentably indistinct before retaining them in one application. If retained, disclosure of plural embodiments does not justify more than a single claim; the claim must be in formal terms (see MPEP §1503.01 III).

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-step analysis for patentable distinctness (appearance + obviousness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the obviousness standard under 35 U.S.C. 103: first determine whether the embodiments have overall appearances that are basically the same as each other; if they are basically the same, determine whether the differences are minor/patentably indistinct or obvious to a designer of ordinary skill in view of analogous prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If embodiments meet both criteria (basically same overall appearance AND differences minor/obvious), they may be retained in one application. If they do not meet either criterion, restriction is required. Note: if overall appearances are not basically the same, restriction must be required even if differences would be obvious in view of prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differences in appearance create patentable distinctness
rubrics_metrics.description: If embodiments do not have overall appearances that are basically the same, restriction must be required since their appearances are patentably distinct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner must include a brief explanation of the differences between the appearances of the embodiments that render them patentably distinct when making a restriction requirement (use appropriate form paragraphs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Differences shown obvious vs differences minor/patentably indistinct
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when overall appearances are basically the same, the differences between embodiments must be either minor and patentably indistinct, or shown to be obvious in view of analogous prior art for the embodiments to be retained together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If differences are minor/patentably indistinct or are shown to be obvious, embodiments are deemed obvious variations and are retained/examined in the same application. Any rejection of one embodiment over prior art will apply equally to all other embodiments in that group; applicants cannot later argue patentability based on those differences if they were determined indistinct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification disclosure requirements for multiple embodiments (written description/antecedent basis)
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification should make clear that multiple embodiments are disclosed and should particularize the differences between the embodiments. If the disclosure of any embodiment relies on the disclosure of another embodiment for completeness to satisfy 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (or pre‑AIA 112, first paragraph), the differences between the embodiments must be identified either in the figure descriptions or by way of a descriptive statement in the specification as filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example language: state that a view 'is a second embodiment of Figure 1, the only difference being the configuration of the door, it being understood that all other surfaces are the same as those of the first embodiment.' In absence of such a statement, one embodiment normally will not provide antecedent basis for amendments to others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination vs subcombination / change in scope test
rubrics_metrics.description: A design claim covers the entire design as a whole and does not extend to any individual part or portion thereof; embodiments directed to a design as a whole (combination) and individual parts (subcombinations) may not be included in a single application if the appearances are patentably distinct. Designs of different scope may be included only if they are patentably indistinct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The difference in scope must be minor and not a patentable distinction; the scope differences must be obvious over one another under 35 U.S.C. 103 without the aid of analogous prior art. If the difference in scope impacts the overall appearance so as to distinguish designs, separate claims (and thus separate applications) are necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction requirement under 35 U.S.C. 121 — election and cancellation
rubrics_metrics.description: When groups of embodiments are patentably distinct, restriction is required under 35 U.S.C. 121 to one of the identified patentably distinct groups of designs. A reply must include an election of a single group for prosecution on the merits, even if the requirement is traversed (37 CFR 1.143). Any reply not including election will be held nonresponsive. Applicant is requested to direct cancellation of drawing figures and corresponding descriptions directed to nonelected groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If applicant traverses the restriction, they should present evidence now of record showing groups to be obvious variations. Failure to present evidence risks the groups being treated as single inventive concept or the reply being nonresponsive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grouping: obvious variations within a group treated as single inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: If embodiments within a group are considered by the examiner to be obvious variations of one another (patentably indistinct), they comprise a single inventive concept and are grouped together; embodiments in different groups are patentably distinct from one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any rejection of one embodiment over prior art will apply equally to all embodiments in the grouped set. Once grouped as a single inventive concept, arguments asserting patentability based on differences between embodiments will not be considered. Failure to traverse is considered admission of lack of patentable distinction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant traverse standard and evidentiary burden
rubrics_metrics.description: Should applicant traverse the restriction requirement on the grounds that the groups are not patentably distinct, applicant should present evidence or identify such evidence now of record showing the groups to be obvious variations of one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If applicant fails to present evidence when traversing, the groups may be deemed patentably distinct and restriction sustained; if later groups are determined not patentably distinct and remain in application, any rejection of one group will apply equally to others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner must include brief explanation of differences when requiring restriction
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners must include a brief explanation of the differences between embodiments that render them patentably distinct in the restriction requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the prescribed form paragraphs (e.g., ¶ 15.27 and subparagraphs) and insert specific explanation(s) of the difference(s) between embodiments (bracketed insertions in form paragraphs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Form paragraph and notice usage (restriction not required / required)
rubrics_metrics.description: Form paragraphs (e.g., 15.27.02/03/04/05/06/07 etc.) may be used to notify applicant whether restriction is required or not and to state the examiner's determination regarding patentable distinctness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select the appropriate paragraph for: Restriction Not Required (change in appearance or scope), Restriction Required (groups identified), Telephone Restriction variations, and include bracketed specifics (embodiment numbers, groups, explanations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional telephone election procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: During a telephone discussion, a provisional election may be made (e.g., to traverse or to elect a group). Affirmation of the provisional election should be made by applicant in replying to the Office action. A group may be withdrawn from further consideration by the examiner as being for a nonelected design(s) (37 CFR 1.142(b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include dates/persons in the record for telephone elections. Examiner notes should be completed with bracketed insertions as required (e.g., insert --with-- or --without-- in the form paragraph).

rubrics_metrics.name: Action on the merits deferred pending compliance with restriction
rubrics_metrics.description: When restriction is required, action on the merits is deferred pending compliance with the requirement in accordance with precedent (e.g., Ex parte Heckman).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner should defer substantive examination until applicant elects and cancels the nonelected groups or otherwise complies with the restriction requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design patent protection does not extend to segregable parts (require separate patents)
rubrics_metrics.description: Design patent protection covers only the design disclosed as an entirety and does not extend to patentably distinct segregable parts; the only way to protect such segregable parts is to apply for separate patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite: Ex parte Sanford; Blumcraft of Pittsburgh v. Ladd. If designs involve segregable parts that are patentably distinct, restriction to one invention is required under 35 U.S.C. 121 and separate claims/applications are necessary to protect parts.
